blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Chemical reactions are classified on the basis of rate in three categories:

• Slow-These reactions occur over extended periods, often taking days, weeks, or even longer to reach completion. Examples include rusting of iron or the decomposition of organic matter.
    • Moderate- These take longer, typically from minutes to hours. Many synthesis reactions and some precipitation reactions fall into this category.
    • Fast- These occur quickly, often in seconds or milliseconds. Examples include combustion and certain acid-base reactions.

rows: Involves ionic speciesTypically completes in seconds
Involves covalent speciesTakes minutes to years

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Explain why rusting of iron is classified as a slow reaction.
blocks.answer: Rusting of iron is a chemical reaction where iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of moisture to form iron oxide (rust). This process involves the oxidation of iron atoms over time. It is classified as a slow reaction because it happens gradually over a long period of time, often taking days, weeks, or even longer depending on environmental conditions like humidity, temperature, and the amount of oxygen present.
blocks.prompt: Explain why rusting of iron is classified as a slow reaction.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Why Acid-base neutralization reactions are very fast reaction ?
blocks.answer: Acid-base neutralization is very fast because it involves a simple and immediate proton transfer between H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, driven by strong electrostatic attraction.

blocks.title: Common Confusions
blocks.text:
• Confusion between the terms rate and speed – "rate" is a broader term that can refer to various types of changes over time and it is quantitative, while "speed" specifically refers to distance travelled over time.
            • Assuming all fast reactions are instantaneous, some may require specific conditions or catalysts.
            • Assuming conditions are constant when they may vary with temperature and other factors.
            • Always consider environmental conditions and the nature of reactants to accurately classify reactions.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Chemical Kinetics: The study of reaction rates and the mechanisms by which they occur. It distinguishes between the feasibility of a reaction (thermodynamics) and its speed of a reaction i.e. time taken by a reaction to reach equilibrium (kinetics).

• Reaction Rate: This is the speed at which reactants are converted to products. It's usually expressed as the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction:

• Concentration: Higher concentration of reactant generally increases reaction rate.

  • Temperature: Typically increases reaction rates but may alter mechanisms.
The reaction rate increases, often by a factor of 2 for every 10°C rise in temperature.

  • Surface Area: Greater surface areas lead to faster reactions.
  • Catalysts: Lower activation energy, increasing reaction rate.

blocks.title: Types of Rate of Reaction
blocks.text:
• Average Rate:

Average rate of reaction refers to the total change in concentration over a specific period of time.

For a reaction R → P

  • $\text{Average rate} = \frac{-\Delta[\text{Reactant}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta[\text{Product}]}{\Delta t}$
Here, [Reactant] or [Product] is the change in concentration of reactants or products, and Δt is the change in time over which the reaction occurs. The negative sign for the reactant's rate signifies that its concentration decreases over time.

• Instantaneous Rate:

Use experimental data to calculate changes in concentration over small time intervals.

For a reaction R → P

  • $\text{Instantaneous rate} = -\frac{d[\text{Reactant}]}{dt} = \frac{d[\text{Product}]}{dt}$
where [Reactant] or [Product]represents the concentration of the substance and dt is time.

The derivative gives the slope of the tangent to the concentration vs. time graph at a specific point, representing the rate at that instant.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Rate of Reaction in the Form of Stoichiometry of a Chemical Reaction.

Let us consider a reaction:

$m_1 \text{A} + m_2 \text{B} \rightarrow n_1 \text{P} + n_2 \text{Q}$

Where,

$\text{Rate of disappearance of A} = -\frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} $, $\text{Rate of disappearance of B} = -\frac{d[\text{B}]}{dt}$

$\text{Rate of appearance of P} = \frac{d[\text{P}]}{dt} $, $\text{Rate of appearance of Q} = \frac{d[\text{Q}]}{dt} $

The Rate of the reaction = $-\frac{1}{m_1} \frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{m_2} \frac{d[\text{B}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{n_1} \frac{d[\text{P}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{n_2} \frac{d[\text{Q}]}{dt}  \text{}$

$\text{Unit of rate of reaction} = \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{time}^{-1} \, \text{i.e.} \, (\text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1} \, $

$\text{or} \, $ $\text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{min}^{-1} \, \text{or} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{h}^{-1})$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
A gaseous hypothetical chemical equation 2A ⇌ B + C is carried out in a closed vessel. The concentration of B is found to increase by $5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{mol L}^{-1}$ in 10 second. The rate of appearance of B is :

$\text{1) } 5 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1} \\  \text{2) } 5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1} \\  \text{3) } 5 \times 10^{-2} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1} \\  \text{4) } 5 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1} $
blocks.answer:
Solution :

$\text{Rate of appearance of } B = \frac{\text{Increase in concentration of } B}{\text{Time taken}} = \frac{5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{mol L}^{-1}}{10 \, \text{sec}} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{sec}^{-1}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
If the reaction $2\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2$, the rate of formation of NO is $6 \, \text{g min}^{-1}$, calculate rate of disappearance of $NO_2$ in $\text{g min}^{-1}$.

$\text{1) } 3.2 \, \text{g min}^{-1} \\ \text{2) } 6.0 \, \text{g min}^{-1} \\ \text{3) } 12.0 \, \text{g min}^{-1} \\ \text{4) } 9.2 \, \text{g min}^{-1}$
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$2\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2 \\ \text{Rate of reaction (ROR)} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Rate of disappearance (ROD) of NO}_2 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Rate of formation (ROF) of NO} = 1 \times \text{ROF of O}_2 \\ \text{ROD of NO}_2 = \frac{2}{2} \times \text{ROF of NO}$

$\text{ROD of NO}_2 = 1 \times \frac{6}{30} \, \text{mol min}^{-1} = 0.2 \, \text{mol min}^{-1} \, \text{(molar mass of NO = 30)}$

$\text{ROD of NO}_2 = 0.2 \times 46 = 9.2 \, \text{g min}^{-1} \, \text{(molar mass of NO}_2 = 46\text{)}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• It's common to confuse reaction rates with equilibrium positions.

• Misinterpretation that while increasing temperature generally speeds up reaction rates but it can also lead to changes in reaction mechanisms.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Rate Law (Experimental concept)- It expresses the relationship between the rate of a chemical reaction and the concentrations of the reactants                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this expression rate of reaction is directly proportional to the product of molar concentration of reactant with each term raised to the power or exponent that has to be found excrementally.

  • For a general elementary reaction $aA + bB \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the rate law is:
$\text{Rate} = k[A]^n[B]^m$
  • k is the rate constant, specific to the reaction at a given temperature.
  • m and n are the order of reactant A and B respectively, and the order of the reaction = m+n determined experimentally.

blocks.title: Mechanisn of Reaction
blocks.text:
Elementary Reactions:

  • Those reactions which completes in single step and which have exponents in rate law equal to
  • stoichiometric coefficients of the reactants.
  • If A + B → Products; is an elementary reaction
  • Rate law will be – Rate = k[A][B]
Complex Reactions:

  • Those reactions which complete in multistep. For these reactions a mechanism is proposed.
  • For complex reactions the overall rate of reaction is controlled by the slowest step which is called as rate determining step (R.D.S.).
  • In rate law expression rate of reaction depends on concentration of reactants of slowest step which must be free from intermediate.
  • If R.D.S. contains intermediate, its value is solved using Keq of fast step (assumed as reversible)
Example-1

$2NO_2Cl → 2NO_2 + Cl_2$$$

Experimentally, the rate law is

$K = [NO_2Cl]$

The mechanism of the reaction is given as –

  •$$$ [NO_2Cl]$ → $NO_2+Cl(Slow reaction)$
• $N{O_2}Cl + Cl \to N{O_2} + C{l_2}(Fast\,\,Step)$
So the rate law from slowest step Rate = $k[N{O_2}Cl]$

In this way the predicted rate law derived from two step mechanism agrees with experimental rate law.

blocks.title: Pseudo First Order Reaction
blocks.text:
• A pseudo-first-order reaction is a reaction that appears to be of first order but actually involves multiple reactants. The order of the reaction is simplified to first order because the concentration of one reactant is much larger than that of the other(s), causing its concentration to remain relatively constant during the reaction. This makes the reaction rate dependent primarily on the concentration of the limiting reactant, simplifying the kinetics.

• For a reaction involving two reactants, A and B, the rate law is generally:
    • $\text{Rate} = k[A]^n[B]^m$
    • For a pseudo-first-order reaction, if the concentration of B is much larger than that of A, [B] remains constant during the reaction. As a result, the rate law becomes:
    • $\text{Rate} = k'[A]$

$k' = k[B]$

which is treated as a constant. This reduces the reaction to first order with respect to A.

• Example: (Acidic hydrolysis of Ester)

$\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$

$H_2O$ is in excess amount. concentration of water will be constant

• Molecularity is 2 and order is 1.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
For a reaction rate law equation is $r = k(C)^{5/2}$. Then unit of rate constant will be:

$\text{1) } \text{mol}^{-3/2} \, \text{L}^{3/2} \, \text{s}^{-1} \\ \text{2) } \text{mol}^{3/2} \, \text{L}^{-3/2} \, \text{s}^{-1} \\ \text{3) } \text{mol}^{-1/2} \, \text{L}^{1/2} \, \text{s}^{-1} \\ \text{4) } \text{mol} \, \text{L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1}$
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$r = k(C)^{5/2} \\ \text{Unit of } k = \frac{\text{unit of } r}{(\text{unit of concentration})^{5/2}} = \frac{\text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{5/2}} \\ = \text{mol}^{-3/2} \, \text{L}^{3/2} \, \text{s}^{-1}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
For the reaction $A + 2B \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the rate law is found to be $\text{Rate} = k[A][B]^2$. Calculate the change in rate if the concentration of A and B both are doubled.

1) The rate will double.
2) The rate will increase by a factor of 4.
3) The rate will increase by a factor of 8.
4) The rate will remain unchanged.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$\text{Initial Rate:} \\ \text{Rate} = k[A][B]^2. \\  \text{New Rate when both } [A] \text{ and } [B] \text{ are doubled:} \\ \text{New Rate} = k(2[A])(2[B])^2 \\  \text{Expanding } (2[B])^2 \text{ gives:} \\ \text{New Rate} = k(2[A]) \cdot 4[B]^2 \\  \text{This simplifies to:} \\ \text{New Rate} = 8 \times k[A][B]^2 = 8 \times \text{Original Rate} \\  \text{Answer:} \\ \text{If both } [A] \text{ and } [B] \text{ are doubled, the rate will increase by a factor of 8.}$

blocks.title: Common Confusions
blocks.text:
• Confusion between rate with rate constant : Remember that the rate varies with concentration, while the rate constant (k) is fixed for a given temperature.
  • Assumption - It is often convenient to assume that the reaction orders (m and n) are equal to the stoichiometric coefficients of the reactants in a balanced chemical equation, this assumption is not always valid. The reaction orders must be determined experimentally.
  • Zero order reactions can never be elementary reactions.
  • For elementary reactions fractional order is not possible.

blocks.title: Order of Reaction
blocks.text:
• The order of a reaction with respect to a particular reactant is the exponent to which its concentration is raised in the rate law expression.

• The overall order of a reaction is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.

• Molecularity of Reaction - The number of molecules that collide in an elementary reaction step.

blocks.title: The differences between order and molecularity

rows: Exponent in the rate law indicating how the rate depends on concentration.
Number of reactant molecules involved in an elementary step.
Can be zero, positive, negative, or fractional (e.g., 0.5, 1.5).
Based on the stoichiometry of elementary reactions.
Reflects the overall relationship between concentration and reaction rate.
Indicates the mechanism of the reaction at a specific step.

blocks.text:
Zero-Order Reaction

    • In a zero-order reaction, the rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of the reactant(s).
First-Order Reaction

  • In a first-order reaction, the rate of reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of one reactant.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Specific Percentages and Corresponding Times in Terms of  $t_{1/2}$ for first order reaction

50% Completion:  $t = t_{1/2}$

75% Completion: $t = 2 \times t_{1/2}$

$t_{90\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(10)}{0.693} \approx 3.32 \, t_{1/2}$

$t_{99.9\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(1000)}{0.693} \approx 9.97 \, t_{1/2}$

$t_{99.99\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(10000)}{0.693} \approx 13.3 \, t_{1/2}$

modules.name: Effect of Temperature and Arrhenius Equation

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: The Arrhenius equation captures the relationship between temperature and reaction rate, with key factors being activation energy, pre-exponential factor, and temperature. By studying this equation, we can predict how the rate of a reaction will change as temperature varies and estimate the activation energy for a reaction.

blocks.title: The Arrhenius Equation
blocks.text:
• The Arrhenius equation illustrates the critical role of temperature and activation energy in determining reaction rates.

It is expressed as:

$k = A e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$

Where:

k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea​ is the activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is the temperature in Kelvin.

(Assumes constant $A$ and $E_a$ over the temperature range)

• Effect of temperature:

Higher temperatures increase reaction rates by raising the rate constant k and enhancing the kinetic energy of molecules, leading to more frequent and effective collisions.

Reactions with higher activation energy Ea​ are more sensitive to temperature changes.

• Linear form of the Arrhenius equation

$\ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{R} \cdot \frac{1}{T}$

This linear form allows for the determination of activation energy Ea by plotting experimental data of k at different temperatures.

$\ln \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = \frac{E_a}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2} \right)$

Where:

$k_1 = \text{rate constant at temperature } T_1$

$k_2 = \text{rate constant at temperature } T_2$

$E_a = \text{activation energy (in J/mol)}$

R=universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol K)

$T_1 \text{ and } T_2 = \text{temperatures (in Kelvin)}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
For first order gaseous reaction log k when plotted against 1/T, gives a straight line with a slope of –8000. Calculate the activation energy of the reaction.

1) 36,660 cal/mol
2) 45,000 cal/mol
3) 28,500 cal/mol
4) 25,000 cal/mol
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$\text{Arrhenius equation: } k = A e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$

$\text{Taking the logarithm of both sides: } \log k = \log A - \frac{E_a}{2.303RT}$

$\text{When the plot is made between } \log k \text{ and } \frac{1}{T}, \text{ we get a straight line}$

$\text{Slope of this line is: } \frac{-E_a}{2.303R}$

$\text{Given that the slope is 8000}$

$\frac{E_a}{2.303R} = 8000$

$\text{Therefore,} \quad E_a = 8000 \times 2.303 \times 1.987 = 36608 \, \text{Cal/mol}$

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
1- Ensure T (temperature) is always in Kelvin and be cautious with unit conversions for R (universal gas constant).

2-For quick calculation: For every 10°C rise, the reaction rate approximately doubles.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Collision Theory: Chemical reactions occur when reactant molecules effectively collide with sufficient energy and correct orientation.

• Catalysis: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction without being consumed by lowering the activation energy.

blocks.title: Effective Collision
blocks.text:
For effective collision following two conditions must be satisfied at a time:

• Reacting molecules must posses a minimum amount of energy.

• Proper orientation of collision

• Threshold energy: The minimum energy which must be possessed by reacting molecules for a chemical reaction to occur.

• Activation energy: The minimum extra amount of energy required by reactant molecules for converting into products.

• Ea(f) = Activation energy for forward reaction

• Ea(b) = Activation energy for backward reaction

If not specified in questions then consider Ea for forward reaction.

blocks.title: Formulas
blocks.text:
• For a bimolecular elementary reaction -    A+B→Products

$\text{Rate} = Z_{AB} e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$

• Rate: Change in concentration over time.
    • Collision frequency ($Z_{AB}$): Number of collisions between A and B per unit time per unit volume.
    • Exponential factor:  $e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$ represents the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea.

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• Activated complex is most unstable complex formed in the transition state with effective collision.

• On increasing temperature Ea for reaction does not decrease but number of active molecules which are crossing the energy barrier increases therefore rate of reaction increases.

Activation Energy Mainly Depends Upon:

• Nature of reactant

• Presence of catalyst.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
An exothermic reaction A → B has an activation energy of 17 kJ mol–1 of A. The heat of the reaction is 40 kJ. Calculate the activation energy for the reverse reaction B → A.

1) 57 kJ/mol
2) 25 kJ/mol
3) 17 kJ/mol
4) 40 kJ/mol
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$\text{For the reaction } \text{A} \rightarrow \text{B}: \\ \text{Activation energy } E_a = 17 \, \text{kJ} \\ \Delta H = -40 \, \text{kJ} \\ \Delta H = E_a(f) - E_a(b) \\ E_a(b) = 17 - (-40) \\ = 57 \, \text{kJ}$

Chemical reactions are classified on the basis of rate in three categories:

• Slow-These reactions occur over extended periods, often taking days, weeks, or even longer to reach completion. Examples include rusting of iron or the decomposition of organic matter.
    • Moderate- These take longer, typically from minutes to hours. Many synthesis reactions and some precipitation reactions fall into this category.
    • Fast- These occur quickly, often in seconds or milliseconds. Examples include combustion and certain acid-base reactions.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Chemical Kinetics: The study of reaction rates and the mechanisms by which they occur. It distinguishes between the feasibility of a reaction (thermodynamics) and its speed of a reaction i.e. time taken by a reaction to reach equilibrium (kinetics).

• Reaction Rate: This is the speed at which reactants are converted to products. It's usually expressed as the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction:

• Concentration: Higher concentration of reactant generally increases reaction rate.

  • Temperature: Typically increases reaction rates but may alter mechanisms.
The reaction rate increases, often by a factor of 2 for every 10°C rise in temperature.

  • Surface Area: Greater surface areas lead to faster reactions.
  • Catalysts: Lower activation energy, increasing reaction rate.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Rate of Reaction in the Form of Stoichiometry of a Chemical Reaction.

Let us consider a reaction:

$m_1 \text{A} + m_2 \text{B} \rightarrow n_1 \text{P} + n_2 \text{Q}$

Where,

$\text{Rate of disappearance of A} = -\frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} $, $\text{Rate of disappearance of B} = -\frac{d[\text{B}]}{dt}$

$\text{Rate of appearance of P} = \frac{d[\text{P}]}{dt} $, $\text{Rate of appearance of Q} = \frac{d[\text{Q}]}{dt} $

The Rate of the reaction = $-\frac{1}{m_1} \frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{m_2} \frac{d[\text{B}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{n_1} \frac{d[\text{P}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{n_2} \frac{d[\text{Q}]}{dt}  \text{}$

$\text{Unit of rate of reaction} = \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{time}^{-1} \, \text{i.e.} \, (\text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{s}^{-1} \, $

$\text{or} \, $ $\text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{min}^{-1} \, \text{or} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} \, \text{h}^{-1})$

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• Activated complex is most unstable complex formed in the transition state with effective collision.

• On increasing temperature Ea for reaction does not decrease but number of active molecules which are crossing the energy barrier increases therefore rate of reaction increases.

Activation Energy Mainly Depends Upon:

• Nature of reactant

• Presence of catalyst.

blocks.title: Common Confusions
blocks.text:
• Confusion between the terms rate and speed – "rate" is a broader term that can refer to various types of changes over time and it is quantitative, while "speed" specifically refers to distance travelled over time.
            • Assuming all fast reactions are instantaneous, some may require specific conditions or catalysts.
            • Assuming conditions are constant when they may vary with temperature and other factors.
            • Always consider environmental conditions and the nature of reactants to accurately classify reactions.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• It's common to confuse reaction rates with equilibrium positions.

• Misinterpretation that while increasing temperature generally speeds up reaction rates but it can also lead to changes in reaction mechanisms.

blocks.title: Common Confusions
blocks.text:
• Confusion between rate with rate constant : Remember that the rate varies with concentration, while the rate constant (k) is fixed for a given temperature.
  • Assumption - It is often convenient to assume that the reaction orders (m and n) are equal to the stoichiometric coefficients of the reactants in a balanced chemical equation, this assumption is not always valid. The reaction orders must be determined experimentally.
  • Zero order reactions can never be elementary reactions.
  • For elementary reactions fractional order is not possible.

blocks.title: Important Points
blocks.text:
• Use proper formula of half-life time for different orders.

• For zero-order linear decrease in concentration over time and for first order exponential decrease in concentration over time.

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
1- Ensure T (temperature) is always in Kelvin and be cautious with unit conversions for R (universal gas constant).

2-For quick calculation: For every 10°C rise, the reaction rate approximately doubles.

blocks.title: Common Confusions
blocks.text:
• Assuming that catalysts change the equilibrium constant of a reaction.

• Confusing activation energy with the overall energy change of the reaction.

blocks.title: Mechanisn of Reaction
blocks.text:
Elementary Reactions:

  • Those reactions which completes in single step and which have exponents in rate law equal to
  • stoichiometric coefficients of the reactants.
  • If A + B → Products; is an elementary reaction
  • Rate law will be – Rate = k[A][B]
Complex Reactions:

  • Those reactions which complete in multistep. For these reactions a mechanism is proposed.
  • For complex reactions the overall rate of reaction is controlled by the slowest step which is called as rate determining step (R.D.S.).
  • In rate law expression rate of reaction depends on concentration of reactants of slowest step which must be free from intermediate.
  • If R.D.S. contains intermediate, its value is solved using Keq of fast step (assumed as reversible)
Example-1

$2NO_2Cl → 2NO_2 + Cl_2$$$

Experimentally, the rate law is

$K = [NO_2Cl]$

The mechanism of the reaction is given as –

  •$$$ [NO_2Cl]$ → $NO_2+Cl(Slow reaction)$
• $N{O_2}Cl + Cl \to N{O_2} + C{l_2}(Fast\,\,Step)$
So the rate law from slowest step Rate = $k[N{O_2}Cl]$

In this way the predicted rate law derived from two step mechanism agrees with experimental rate law.

blocks.title: The Arrhenius Equation
blocks.text:
• The Arrhenius equation illustrates the critical role of temperature and activation energy in determining reaction rates.

It is expressed as:

$k = A e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$

Where:

k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea​ is the activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is the temperature in Kelvin.

(Assumes constant $A$ and $E_a$ over the temperature range)

• Effect of temperature:

Higher temperatures increase reaction rates by raising the rate constant k and enhancing the kinetic energy of molecules, leading to more frequent and effective collisions.

Reactions with higher activation energy Ea​ are more sensitive to temperature changes.

• Linear form of the Arrhenius equation

$\ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{R} \cdot \frac{1}{T}$

This linear form allows for the determination of activation energy Ea by plotting experimental data of k at different temperatures.

$\ln \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = \frac{E_a}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2} \right)$

Where:

$k_1 = \text{rate constant at temperature } T_1$

$k_2 = \text{rate constant at temperature } T_2$

$E_a = \text{activation energy (in J/mol)}$

R=universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol K)

$T_1 \text{ and } T_2 = \text{temperatures (in Kelvin)}$

blocks.title: Formulas
blocks.text:
• For a bimolecular elementary reaction -    A+B→Products

$\text{Rate} = Z_{AB} e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$

• Rate: Change in concentration over time.
    • Collision frequency ($Z_{AB}$): Number of collisions between A and B per unit time per unit volume.
    • Exponential factor:  $e^{-\frac{E_a}{RT}}$ represents the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea.

blocks.title: Effective Collision
blocks.text:
For effective collision following two conditions must be satisfied at a time:

• Reacting molecules must posses a minimum amount of energy.

• Proper orientation of collision

• Threshold energy: The minimum energy which must be possessed by reacting molecules for a chemical reaction to occur.

• Activation energy: The minimum extra amount of energy required by reactant molecules for converting into products.

• Ea(f) = Activation energy for forward reaction

• Ea(b) = Activation energy for backward reaction

If not specified in questions then consider Ea for forward reaction.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Rate Law (Experimental concept)- It expresses the relationship between the rate of a chemical reaction and the concentrations of the reactants                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      In this expression rate of reaction is directly proportional to the product of molar concentration of reactant with each term raised to the power or exponent that has to be found excrementally.

  • For a general elementary reaction $aA + bB \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the rate law is:
$\text{Rate} = k[A]^n[B]^m$
  • k is the rate constant, specific to the reaction at a given temperature.
  • m and n are the order of reactant A and B respectively, and the order of the reaction = m+n determined experimentally.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Specific Percentages and Corresponding Times in Terms of  $t_{1/2}$ for first order reaction

50% Completion:  $t = t_{1/2}$

75% Completion: $t = 2 \times t_{1/2}$

87.5% Completion: $t = 3 \times t_{1/2}$

93.75% Completion: $t = 4 \times t_{1/2}$

$t_{90\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(10)}{0.693} \approx 3.32 \, t_{1/2}$

$t_{99\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(100)}{0.693} \approx 6.64 \, t_{1/2}$

$t_{99.9\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(1000)}{0.693} \approx 9.97 \, t_{1/2}$

$t_{99.99\%} = t_{1/2} \cdot \frac{\ln(10000)}{0.693} \approx 13.3 \, t_{1/2}$
